It should be stated that the phrase in the subsequent text, "Knowing they were weary and lax, he manifested a city for them," refers precisely to the "seeking."

Alternatively, it may be interpreted that the chariot symbolizes *anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana without remainder); because the fruit has not yet been attained while dwelling therein, one must seek it. The city symbolizes *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana with remainder); because the fruit has already been attained while dwelling therein, one does not seek it.

If that is so, since the bodhisattvas have now requested the vehicle, they must already possess the remainder [of suffering] and not yet have attained the remainderless [nirvāṇa]; it is because they seek the remainderless state that they are said to "request" it.
As for the two vehicles, since their remainderless attainment is certain to occur spontaneously, why would they need to cultivate such a request?
Therefore, one should simply follow the meaning previously stated: since the nirvāṇa spoken of is without distinction for the two vehicles, the sheep and deer carts should not exist.
As the Sūtra says: "Śāriputra, [you shall all ride] upon the single great carriage of equality."
The commentary states:
This passage concerns the gift of a single [chariot], which is divided into four parts:
first, the presentation of the chariot; second, the description of its adornments; third, the manifestation of the ox's characteristics; and fourth, the display of the attendants.
This is the first [point].
The ox-cart of the Buddha-fruit has the "knowledge of all modes" (*sarvākārajñatā*) among the four wisdoms as its nature; that is, it is the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).
The causal cart has the "knowledge of all modes" within the two wisdoms—the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*) and the wisdom of equality (*samatā-jñāna*)—as its essence.
Although the five wisdoms are all of the One Vehicle, here we take only the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) within the aspect of bodhi as the essence.

While the "knowledge of all things" (*sarvajñatā*) differs in breadth and narrowness and is shared by the three vehicles, this "knowledge of all modes" distinguishes the four truths into each of their infinite aspects;
it is a unique quality (*asādhāraṇa-guṇa*) unknown to the two vehicles. Therefore, the Sūtra says:
It has been stated several times that "one shall ultimately cause [beings] to attain all-aspect wisdom" (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) guides this vehicle of all-aspect wisdom; the meaning is as previously explained: the ox is not the actual body of the vehicle.

Just as both the manifest (*vijñapti*) and unmanifest (*avijñapti*) are equally precepts, yet when receiving them from the Saṃgha and during subsequent observance, only the unmanifest is mentioned—so too is the case with the manifest precept for a single moment.

It is not a continuous [process], because it is obtained through the harmony of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*, and because the informative act (*vijñapti*) has already been completed at the time of requesting it from the Saṃgha.
Although the informative act is the primary basis, it is only the non-informative act (*avijñapti*) that is designated as "upholding" or "violating" the precepts.

This chariot is likewise. Although the preceding "Great Matter" took both principle-wisdom (*li-zhi*) and wisdoms—both original wisdom (*ben-zhi*) and subsequent wisdom (*hou-zhi*)—as a single vehicle (*ekayāna*), here we take only subsequent wisdom as the chariot and original wisdom as the ox; we do not describe principle itself as the body of the chariot. In the later city of transformation, the true is contrasted with the transformative: there, conventional analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is described as the city of transformation, while the wondrous principle of True Suchness (*tathatā*) within Great Nirvāṇa is described as the precious destination. Each is called a "single vehicle" based on its own specific meaning, because the vehicles of phenomena (*dharma-yāna*) and principle (*li-yāna*), and the vehicles of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-yāna*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-yāna*), are distinct.
The body of the sheep-cart and the deer-cart has already been analyzed as before. Since that is the case for the bodies of the carts, the remaining myriad virtues belong to their adornments.

If one follows the explanations in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and the *Śrīmālādevī Siṃhanāda Sūtra*, which take only True Suchness (*tathatā*) as the body of the cart, how could each of the sons be given a single cart?
Furthermore, how can it be said that there are distinct qualities that adorn his appearance? How could an ox-drawn carriage be as swift as the wind?
And how can it be said, "I possess such great seven-jeweled carriages, immeasurable in number, which I ought to give to each with an impartial mind"?

However, once the younger and middle sons have also gone out the gate, although they have not yet obtained the ox-carts, the Great Teaching is preached for them; thus, it may certainly be said that they have been "given" [the carts]. This is because, at that time, they have already attained the essence of the wisdom that is the referent [of the teaching], even if they have not yet physically received the precious pearl. Therefore, the three kinds of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*) mentioned in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* and other texts are precisely these three sons.
This explains that the first stage (*bhūmi*) is called the "Stage of Non-retrogression.

Furthermore, regarding the sudden awakening of those who practice the causal path of the Mahāyāna: although from the initial generation of the mind one may also be said to be on a "vehicle," here we specifically take the causal practice of non-retrogression from the eighth stage onward. Prior to the seventh stage, there is still the existence of fragmented birth-and-death (*saṃvṛta-jāti*). Therefore, the sutra below states: "Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas mount this precious vehicle and proceed directly to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*)," because the *Upāya-paryāya* chapter explains that entering [this stage] is precisely the stage of non-retrogression.

Now, adopting the former interpretation: from the first bhūmi upward, one is free from death by fragmentation and is thus called the "Non-retrogressive Stage" (*avaivartika-bhūmi*) and is said to "ride the One Vehicle. This is because the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states that from the first bhūmi upward, one is called the "threefold mind-made body" (*manomaya-kāya*).
The Sūtra says: "The chariot was high and wide, with bells suspended on all four sides.
The commentary states:
The following clarifies the ornamental adornments, which are tenfold:
This section contains four parts: first, size and form;
second, adornment; third, control; and fourth, bells and chimes. "High and broad" refers to size and form.

This metaphorically illustrates that the essence of the Buddha’s knowledge of all modes is high, transcending the three realms, while its function is broad, extending throughout the ten directions; for it is capable of both illuminating and transforming, pervading the entire dharma-realm.
"Adorned with various jewels" refers to magnificent ornamentation; because it is accomplished through square virtues, wisdom serves as its foundation.

"Surrounded by railings" refers to restraint and governance: restraining the external so that nothing enters and governing the internal so that nothing escapes. This corresponds to the four *dhāraṇīs*, which govern all evils so they do not arise and govern all virtues so they do not disperse.
"Chimes suspended on all four sides" refers to *ghaṇṭā* (bells); they pervade the four modes of birth, proclaiming the sevenfold eloquence to provide universal salvation.
The Sūtra says: "Furthermore, upon it, [one should] adorn it with... and so forth.
The commentary states:
This consists of two types of adornment:
five high canopies and six clusters of brilliance.
"Spreading out canopies and awnings" refers to high coverage; because the four immeasurables provide broad shelter for all living beings like a canopy and awning.

"Various adornments" refers to manifold brilliance; for loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity each possess various practices—whether directed toward sentient beings, phenomena, or the objectless—which serve as auxiliary adornments.
Regarding the passage from "interlaced with jeweled cords" to "placed upon rafts and boats," the commentary states:
This consists of four adornments.
Seventh, the interlacing cords; eighth, the hanging necklaces; ninth, the spread bedding; tenth, the placed pillows.
"Interlacing cords" refers to the Four Great Vows.
In all that one practices, one must first give rise to these four great vows:
First, by means of these roots of goodness, one makes the vow that all sentient beings may together be freed from suffering for those who have not yet left it.
Second, one vows that those who have not yet attained happiness may attain happiness.
Third, one vows that those who have not yet resolved upon bodhicitta and who do not abandon evil to cultivate goodness may resolve upon bodhicitta and abandon evil to cultivate goodness.

Fourth, for those who have not yet attained Buddhahood, may they quickly achieve it; may their various practices be like precious cords interlaced so that they shall surely attain the fruit, being so superior and certain that the violent winds of false views cannot overturn or damage them.
Furthermore, the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* states: "Upholding the True Dharma encompasses all vows.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and other texts state: "In general, there are two types of vows:
the vow to seek enlightenment and the vow to bring benefit and happiness to others."
"Hanging down flower tassels" refers to the hanging of tassels.
This represents the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*), which hang down to gather in the four modes of birth:
first, giving; second, kind speech; third, beneficial conduct; and fourth, cooperation.
The character "huā" has two pronunciations:
*huā* and *huá*. In the phrase "adorned with flowers," it refers to the decoration of a sash with flowers, or a sash that is itself decorated with flowers.
Regarding the phrase "layered and elegantly spread," "fū" (敷) means to arrange or set out.

Some write "quanyan" (綩綖); according to the *Zilin*, the character "quan" (綩) has the phonetic value of "yi-yuan" (一遠反). The *Yupian* states that "quan" means "heng" (紘), and "heng" refers to the crown (guān).

Now, one should write "wan" (婉) for elegant and beautiful prose; as for "yan" (綖), it refers to a mat or cushion and should be written as "xian" (莚). According to the *Qieyun*, "yan means the covering atop a crown," and the *Yupian* states, "that which hangs before and behind a crown is called yan."

Now, taking such things as patterned silk and embroidered woolen rugs to serve as mats and bedding, one does not know from what principle this derives; therefore, the character should properly be written with the radicals for "graceful" (婉) and "extensive" (莚).
There is an ancient interpretation which states that *dhyāna* (meditative concentration) is like a cushion because the mind always rests securely upon it;
since the four *dhyānas* differ in their upper and lower stages, they are called "layered coverings.
This reasoning is incorrect.
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states:

"The four dhyānas serve as the bed, and pure livelihood serves as the bedding. When the actions of body, speech, and mind are all free from greed, and one constantly dwells therein having resolved the mind, always practicing pure livelihood while remaining aloof from the five types of wrong livelihood—such that the three karmas are likewise so—it is called "the layered spread."
"Placing a vermilion pillow" means placing a cushion.

While ancient interpretations held that *nirvāṇa* can bring rest to birth and death, the present explanation holds that the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) can bring rest to discursive攀缘 (*pān-yuan*, cognitive grasping). It is called a "resting pillow" because leaning upon it relieves fatigue; since it is placed upon a carriage, it is clear this is not *nirvāṇa*, but refers instead to the meditative absorption of cessation.
An elixir of immortality is contained within the pillow; by resting upon it, one’s lifespan is increased, and thus it is called a "pillow of elixir.
The meditative absorption of cessation free from outflows is likewise so named because it increases the noble path.
This principle is not otherwise.
Regarding the phrase "the Western Regions have no such thing":
it refers to a pillow that is red in color, stuffed with cotton or layered silk inside and covered with red leather on the outside; thus it is called a "vermilion pillow" (*danzhen*).
There is also an interpretation which states that its substance consists of the five faculties, such as untainted faith (*anāsrava-śraddhā*), which support the noble ones (*ārya*) just like a pillow.
The Sūtra says: "Yoked with white oxen, they proceed as swiftly as the wind.
The commentary states:
The following section reveals the characteristics of the oxen, which are sevenfold:

The single white ox represents the fundamental non-conceptual wisdom (*mūla-nirvikalpa-jñāna*), which guides the chariot of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*); it is like an ox pulling a chariot.
"White" is the source of all colors; thus, it symbolizes the sūtras, as they are the foundation of all vehicles (*yāna*) and the masters of all virtues.
The Bull-King possesses three virtues:
first, the virtue of subduing enmity, because he is able to sever the two hindrances;
second, the virtue of majestic dignity, because he is adorned with all virtues.
Third is the virtue of transport, because it delivers both oneself and others. Therefore, it is compared to an ox rather than an elephant or a horse;

for while a horse is like the Mahāyāna—noble and swift—it cannot be compared to the dullness of the donkey-cart of the Hīnayāna. Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says, "A cart is drawn by a horse. As for the elephant, because its physical form and virtue are great, it is superior to the small physical forms and virtues of the ox, deer, and sheep; and since non-abiding nirvāṇa (*apratisthita-nirvāṇa*) is the most excellent, the *Śīla-samvara Sūtra* employs the elephant to draw the cart.
Now, because the ox possesses three virtues, the Great Vehicle is drawn by white oxen.
Its two flanks are full, for within the midst of right wisdom, its internal virtues are perfected.
The three colors are pure, for the three obstructions are forever exhausted due to the perfection of the virtue of precepts.
Fourth, the physical form is beautiful; according to the *Zilin*, "shu" (姝) denotes a beautiful appearance.

The *Fangyan* states that in the regions of Zhao, Wei, Yan, and Dai, "shu" (姝) is used to mean "beautiful. The *Shijing* says, "The quiet girl is shu," and its commentary, as well as the *Yupian*, defines "shu" as "exquisite beauty. There are also instances where the character "zhu" (侏) is used; in this sense, it means "to be excellent" or "to be good."
The character "Good" (hǎo) is pronounced with the initial *lǎo* (i.e., *hǎo*). It signifies that which is virtuous, appropriate, and beautiful.
Because his marks (*lakṣaṇa*) are perfect and radiant, he is revered and loved by humans and devas.
He possesses the five great powers of strength; in a single stride he can travel anywhere, and his wisdom and power are all-pervasive, exhausting no principle.
Second, they do not grow weary when traversing perils; they are able to transform the ten directions and enter the perils of birth and death without any fatigue.
Third, they are certain to triumph whenever they encounter enemies, for they shatter all obstacles and subdue birth and death.
Possessing these three meanings is called "great physical strength.
Sixth, the gait is level and upright; second, the two principles provide dual verification, guiding the arising of subsequent knowledge, for there is no distinction between enemy and friend.

Seventh, its swiftness is like the wind: the essence of right wisdom universally contemplates the dharma-realm within a single kṣaṇa; bound by great compassion, it internally perfects all virtues and externally transforms all sentient beings, for there is no delay or stagnation.

From the first bhūmi upward, one is able to swiftly cultivate the contemplations of emptiness and existence without delay; thus, although the nature [of these qualities] is sharp and keen, their manifestation is composed and dignified.
Among these seven virtues above, some are not fundamental; rather, they are so named because the function of right knowledge arises through them.
The Sūtra says: "Furthermore, he is attended and guarded by many servants.
The Commentary states:

The following clarifies the retinue. Taking the two wisdoms as the precursor, the myriad practices, supernormal powers, the six perfections, the four means of attraction, the factors of enlightenment, the liberations, and the dharmas for benefiting sentient beings through the afflictions all arise in accordance with them; these are called the "many servants."
Furthermore, the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* states: "The Buddha is constantly attended by immeasurable devas, nāgas, yakṣas, humans, non-humans, and others," who are also called his attendants.

Some interpret the body of the chariot as being solely the Great Parinirvāṇa, while the remaining ornaments are either the qualities of nature (*dharmatā-guṇa*) or the qualities of manifestation (*lakṣaṇa-guṇa*).
The body of the ox, on the other hand, is the two types of wisdom (*jñāna*), for it draws the chariot.
The previous interpretation is correct; as has already been refuted above.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "Why is this so? to "all are completely filled," the commentary says:
The third section explains the fulfillment of the father’s intent; it has three parts:
first, the indication of his wealth; second, the thought of impartiality; and third, the explanation of the reason for this.
This is the first part.
"Filled" means overflowing.

It refers to the capacity of the various treasuries—both conditioned and unconditioned—to contain their respective meanings; or, it refers to how the two or three baskets of the Teaching can contain the underlying principles. Now, we take what is stored therein to provide for all the sons.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from “and he forms this thought” to “it is not appropriate to differentiate,” the Commentary states:
This thought of impartiality is twofold:
"At first one should not give small things, but later one should give all great things.
The passage beginning with "Now this young child" refers to conceptualized mental constructions (*parikalpita*).
"Infinite" (*wuji*) means that there is no limit or end.
The teaching of the two kinds of wisdom is called the "inferior vehicle.
Because they possess the spiritual lineage (*gotra*) and have previously resolved upon the Great Mind (*mahācitta*), they are called "infants";
because they are capable of attaining Buddhahood, they are called "my children."
Compassion that is non-dual is called impartial love.
Adorned with the seven noble riches, it is called the chariot of the seven jewels.

As each person cultivates wisdom to perfection, and since conditioned wisdom is not of a single kind, its varieties are said to be immeasurable; therefore, one should maintain an impartial mind, bestowing according to the faculties of others—this is called "giving to each"—and should universally bestow the Mahāyāna without making distinctions.
The character "tóng" (童) is pronounced with the rhyme *dú hóng*.
What is now called a "tóngzi" (童子, child/pupil) was called a "pú" (僕, servant) in antiquity.
In ancient times, the character "tóng" (僮) was used; what is now called a "pólì" (僕隸, slave/servant) was [then] referred to by that term.
The *Yupian* states: "‘You-tong’ (幼童) is a designation for one who is deluded and ignorant and has not yet undergone the capping ceremony.
From the passage in the Sūtra beginning with "For what reason? up to "How much more so for my sons," the commentary says:
This is the reason for the explanation.
"Deprivation" means exhaustion.

If this One Vehicle were bestowed universally upon all sentient beings of the five destinies within a single Buddha-field—whether they possess the nature [for enlightenment], lack it, or have a fixed or unfixed lineage—it would still not be exhausted; how much less so when given only to the true sons of the Buddha who possess the Mahāyāna nature or an unfixed lineage? Would one fear it being insufficient?
Regarding the sūtra passage, "At that time, the sons arrived at what they had not originally expected," the commentary states:
This is the fourth [stage], which transcends the sons' original minds.

Since it is stated that they each "mount" [the vehicle], it is clearly understood that each attains their own *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge), unlike the case of the illusory city where the multitude entered together.
This is as the Sūtra says: "Śāriputra, [this is] up to the point of being false."
The commentary states: The preceding analogy establishes the reality; the following analogy resolves doubts.

This refers to what was said in the previous fascicle: "You all should have faith and understanding in that which the Buddha has spoken; his words are not false. This was said because the assembly had harbored doubts, asking:
The Buddha initially taught three [vehicles], but later taught only one; since the earlier and later teachings differ, how could the Buddha not be a person who speaks falsely?
Therefore, this is explained as follows.
The text contains three sections:
first, the question; second, the answer;
and third, the seal of approval. This is the first.
Regarding the sūtra passage from “Śāriputra... it is not false,” the commentary states:
The subsequent response consists of two parts.
This consists of an initial statement followed by an explanation;
this is the statement.

Ordinary beings who have abandoned desire and suppressed their afflictions are said to have "escaped the calamity of fire"; those who have left behind the extreme suffering and oppression of the three evil realms are said to have "preserved their bodies and lives. However, they have not yet escaped the human and celestial realms, and thus they have not yet fully preserved their bodies and lives within the burning house.
The character "miǎn" (免) has the phonetic reading *mángbiàn* (亡辨反); it means to expel. According to the *Yùpiān*, it also means to pardon, to release, to liberate, and to depart.
Here, we follow the *Yùpiān*.
Regarding the Sūtra passage from “For what reason? up to “...and deliver them,” the commentary states:
The subsequent explanation has two parts.
First, it is no mere falsehood that one has escaped calamity; second, how much more so when this is granted through the Mahāyāna.
This is the first point.

Merely to preserve one's body and life, emerge from the three evil realms, and be born among humans or devas is already to have encountered a rare treasure; how much more so to escape calamity and be pulled out from the burning house of the human and celestial realms within the triple world.
The Sūtra says: “World-Honored One, [the Tathāgata] is without falsehood.
The commentary states:
Regarding the subsequent comparison with the Mahāyāna, there are two points:
At the outset, it cannot be considered even a minor falsehood, because it does not contradict their prior intention;
how much less so when they subsequently attain the Mahāyāna, which would result in the fault of their [previous claim] being proven false.
This is the first point.
The first part provides the thesis, and the latter part offers the explanation.

Regarding "the initial intention," this refers to a provisional assumption: it was promised that the three vehicles would be given; thus, although they do not currently obtain the Lesser Vehicle, this does not contradict the original provisional intent.
Since the mind and its objects do not contradict one another, it is not established as false.
Regarding the Sūtra passage, "How much more so for the elder... [bestowing] equal great chariots," the commentary says:
How much more so for one who has attained the Mahāyāna—how could they then produce what is false?
The Sūtra says: “The Buddha told Śāriputra... up to ‘as you have said.
The commentary states:
This is the seal of approval.
From the passage in the Sūtra beginning with “Śāriputra... the Father of the World,” the commentary states:
The second major section, which provides a combined exposition, has two parts:
first, the combination of the former provisional [teachings], and second, the combination of the present ultimate reality.
The passage beginning with "Śāriputra! Just as that elder saw his sons safely emerge... constitutes this section.
The initial section has four parts:

first, the convergence of the Buddhas of the three realms; second, from "In order to deliver sentient beings from birth and old age" onwards, the convergence regarding the perils and deaths of the five destinies; third, from "Seeing all sentient beings [afflicted] by birth, old age, sickness, and death" onwards, the convergence regarding the manifestation of skillful means; fourth, "Śāriputra!"... [and so forth].
"If there are sentient beings who possess the nature of wisdom within," and so forth, concludes the section on "relying on words to avoid calamity.
The initial parable consists of six elements:
first, the location; second, the head of the household; third, the old and the young; fourth, the assets; fifth, the features of the residence; and sixth, the doors and windows.
Now there are five things that should be joined together, yet the doors and windows should not be joined.
This passage has two parts:
first, all worldly things that are joined in their locations; second, the father who joins with the head of the household.

"World" (*loka*) refers to both the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*) and the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*). As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "The realm of all sentient beings is the bodhisattva’s purified buddha-field. Therefore, these two types of worlds are designated as the Buddha-land.
"Man is the root of the state; when the root is firm, the state is at peace, and thus one may illuminate and dwell throughout the world.

"Father" carries the meaning of giving birth and nurturing; because he causes all sentient beings to grow their roots of goodness and succeeds to the position of the Buddha-father, he is called "father."
Regarding the sūtra passage from “in all fears” up to “immeasurable knowledge and vision,” the commentary states:
This concludes the third section, which consolidates the assets.
This combines multiple fields: "the exhaustion of fear and so forth" combines the field of abandonment; "immeasurable knowledge and vision" combines the field of wisdom.
There are five kinds of fear:
first, the fear of not being able to sustain oneself, which arises from the conceptualization of a self and attachment to one's livelihood.
Second is the fear of ill repute, which arises from the apprehension that one's harmful conduct will lead to dread;
third is the fear of death, which arises from the perception of a self and the thought of its destruction;
fourth is the fear of the miserable realms, which arises from evil karma when one fails to encounter the Buddhas.

The five fears of the timid, upon seeing them, give rise to the distress and afflictions of inferior realization and being surpassed by others—namely, the various sufferings such as the ruin of one's family and total extinction.

The above collectively describes the fruits of suffering within birth and death (*saṃsāra*), because they are characterized by the increase of the darkness of ignorance and delusion, and because they are the root of afflictions and karma.

"This is the cause of suffering" refers to the failure to understand the past, future, and present; these are respectively correlated with ignorance (*avidyā*) and obscuration, or alternatively, with delusion regarding the Three Jewels, which are correlated in that same order.

Because one realizes the principle and cuts off afflictions so that they are forever exhausted without remainder, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) perfection of the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*) is attained, thereby accomplishing the fulfillment of the virtue of knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana-guṇa*).
Regarding the passage from "The Powers and Fearlessnesses" up to "The Perfections," the commentary states:

Below, this corresponds to immeasurable wealth; internally, the virtues of wisdom and skillful means are both fully perfected, for they have reached the other shore. Thus, everything above constitutes the accumulation of assets.
If one follows the *Vimalakīrti*, afflictions serve as servants;
or, according to this text, supernatural powers used for external transformation serve as servants, because they are driven by wisdom, and thus it is so described.
The Sūtra says: "With great kindness and great compassion, constantly seeking virtuous matters.
The commentary states:
The fourth [section] corresponds to his advanced age.

Because his compassionate regard for the elderly grows ever deeper, he possesses great kindness and great compassion; because his actions are never abandoned, he is always free from weariness; for everything he does, he deliberates, examines, and observes with thoroughness, beginning well and finishing well without any interruption in between; thus, he is dedicated to establishing the supreme Dharma and constantly seeks out virtuous deeds.
Herein, the virtues of gratitude, severance, and wisdom are explained, which correspond respectively to the three types of elders mentioned above.
These represent the long-cultivated causes that benefit both self and others, as compassion and wisdom have been perfected.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "Benefiting All" to "the Decaying Fire-House," the commentary states:
The fifth [section] corresponds to the characteristic of a single house, yet it also corresponds to many houses, because it pervades the three realms.

For the sake of benefiting those in the five destinies, he manifests birth among them; thus, the previous analogy states, "If I and my children do not emerge in a timely manner," which means he manifests dwelling within birth and death for the sake of sentient beings, and manifests emerging from the house only in this present life—this explains the reason for entering the house.

There is also an interpretation which states that "benefit" refers to the doors and windows; because the Buddha enters the house for the sake of benefiting [beings], sentient beings exit the house by relying on that benefit—this is because it pertains to the teaching and practice of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna).
The Sūtra states: “In order to deliver sentient beings, [he proceeds] to *samyaksambodhi*.
The commentary says:
The second major section corresponds to the analogy of the perils and destruction of the five destinies. This primary analogy consists of four parts:
There are four [analogies]: first, a multitude; second, a dilapidated house; third, the arising of calamities;
and fourth, the dwelling of children. Now, these are combined into four as well:

first, the vast multitude of people is combined with the need to deliver sentient beings; second, the perilous decay of the household is combined with birth, old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, and affliction; third, the fires of the three poisons obscured by the darkness of ignorance are combined with the arising of calamities in all directions; and fourth, the teaching and transformation that leads to the fruit of *samyak-saṃbodhi* is combined with the dwelling and wandering of sentient beings.

Birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction are metaphors for impermanence and suffering within the four aggregates; likewise, every dilapidated and decaying dwelling possesses birth, old age, sickness, and death.

If one assigns [the elements] in sequential order, the meaning becomes somewhat difficult to understand, as the faults within a dilapidated house may actually apply to the decay of a dwelling throughout the three realms; therefore, the assignment to the four aggregates is as explained previously.

Now, by means of the faults of the four characteristics of flux within the desire realm, the suffering of the three realms is made manifest; for the sake of causing sentient beings to develop a profound weariness toward birth, old age, sickness, and death, one speaks of the faults of the house’s destruction through birth, old age, sickness, and death.

If this were not so, why would it be that while calamities arise in all directions, and the dwellings of the afflictions common to the three realms are universally dilapidated and decaying, only the bitter fruits of the desire realm are clarified?
As for the phrase "among the sons who roam and dwell, there is one of great lineage," this refers to the true son born of the householder’s wife.
Prior to the arousal of the bodhicitta, one is called a child of the triple world; after the arousal of the mind, one gradually attains bodhi.
As the Sūtra says: "Seeing all sentient beings... undergoing various kinds of suffering."
The commentary states: The third major section of the following text demonstrates the establishment of skillful means. It corresponds to the preceding parable and contains four parts:

first, the arising of compassion upon seeing suffering; second, the demonstration of the Great [Vehicle] while not seeking it for oneself; third, contemplating skillful means to deliver and rescue others; and fourth, the formal exposition of the Three Vehicles.
This conjunction also has four parts:
first, the conjunction with the arising of compassion;
second, "Śāriputra!... [and so forth].
Having seen this, the Buddha then thought: "I am the father of sentient beings. [The following section] below collectively demonstrates the vastness of his lack of expectation.
Third: "Śāriputra!"
The passage beginning with "Just as that elder, although his body and hands possessed strength, did not employ it" corresponds to the contemplation of the means for deliverance.
The fourth section, beginning with "And he spoke these words: 'Do not take pleasure in dwelling within the triple world,'" corresponds to the formal exposition of the Three Vehicles.
The first simile contains two parts:
first, the arising of compassion; second, the object of that compassion.
Herein, the phrase "seeing all sentient beings" corresponds to the arising of compassion.
The passage beginning with "for the sake of birth, old age, sickness, and death" correlates with the objects of compassion.

Within these objects of compassion, the first part correlates with the characteristic of suffering (*duḥkha-lakṣaṇa*), and the latter part correlates with attachment to pleasure. The section beginning with "sentient beings are submerged therein" correlates with the characteristic of suffering; here, the seven sufferings of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are first explained, followed by the phrase "such various kinds of sufferings as these," which explains the form and formless realms (*rūpa- and ārūpyadhātu*).
In both the form and formless realms, the eighth [type of suffering] is fully present; it briefly subsumes all the suffering of the five aggregates of grasping (*pañcopādānaskandha*).
It is explained that there are four types of suffering in the desire realm:

first, the mutual encroachment of the four elements; second, the conflict and competition of the five desires; third, the burning oppression of stinginess and greed; and fourth, the transmigration through the various realms of existence.
The first three are the suffering of the present life, while the latter one is the suffering of future lives.

Furthermore, these four intersecting and overlapping states constitute the four types of suffering: the conflict and rivalry over the five desires and the burning torment of stinginess and greed constitute the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks; the cycle of rebirth within the five destinies clarifies the suffering of separation from the beloved, the suffering of encountering the hateful, and various other manifold sufferings, which briefly encompass the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*). In this way, all eight types of suffering are fully subsumed.
This passage refers to the mutual encroachment of the four modes of birth and the conflicting competition for the five desires.

In the preceding analogy, one’s mind was startled by seeing fire as the cause; here, in this application, one’s heart is moved to compassion by seeing suffering as the fruit. As these states manifest and provoke one another, both are lamentable; as both the prior cause and the subsequent fruit are oppressive, both are pitiable, and both are to be loathed. Thus, the *Abhidharma* states: "Birth is suffering because it is the basis for all sufferings and because it is oppressed by all sufferings."

During the ninth and tenth months while dwelling within the womb, one endures various sufferings such as cold and heat, as if in a pit of excrement; between the stomach and the large intestine, it is like being squeezed between two mountains; as one moves toward the birth canal, the suffering is unbearable; upon emerging, one is buffeted by the wind as if being cut with knives or pierced by needles, involuntarily letting out cries and forgetting all previous activities—this is called the suffering of birth.

The suffering of old age consists in the suffering caused by the transformation of time: the body becomes heavy, the faculties grow dull and dim, the skin slackens and wrinkles, and one's gait becomes hunched. One finds no peace in sleep or eating; rising and sitting involves groaning and labored breathing as the breath becomes obstructed. One’s actions become slow and sluggish, leading others to hold one in contempt. As worldly sentiments deepen and all worldly affairs cease, this is called the suffering of old age.

Regarding the suffering of illness: because the four great elements undergo transformation and lose their harmony, there is suffering; the hundred joints ache and the four limbs are tormented, capable of destroying all matters of peace and well-being, just as hail damages seedlings and suddenly ruins their flourishing growth.

As this sutra states: "Suppose there is a man who, being strong and handsome, secretly loves a royal consort and sends messengers for illicit intercourse. The king captures him, plucks out his eyes, cuts off his ears and nose, and amputates his hands and feet. His appearance is instantly transformed, and he becomes loathed by men; already beset by the unbearable suffering of illness, he is further reviled by others—this is called the suffering of illness."

As for the suffering of death: it is suffering because the life-span undergoes transformation and decay; as the "wind-blade" (vāyu-śastra) dissects the limbs and joints, there is no part that does not experience excruciating pain. The mouth gapes and one heaves deep sighs; hands and feet flail about in confusion; the eyes roll upward and one chews at froth while clutching at empty space; sweat flows profusely, and excrement and mucus fall in a chaotic mixture.

The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Death is like being in a perilous and difficult place where there are no provisions; the destination is far away and one has no companion. One travels day and night without ever knowing its limit; it is deep and dark with no light. There is no gate through which to enter and no dwelling place. Although there is no site of pain, it cannot be healed; there is no stopping on the way, and upon arrival, one finds no release. It is not something that can be destroyed, yet those who witness it are filled with grief and bitterness. It is not an ugly form, yet it causes people to tremble with fear. A cry is at one's ear, yet it cannot be perceived—this is called the suffering of death."

"Though one may temporarily borrow [the body] for bathing, it must ultimately return to impurity; though one may temporarily use it to apply ointments and incense, it must ultimately return to foulness and stench. At that time, the sovereign rank, wealth, treasures, glory, and prosperity, as well as the billions of kinsmen, wives, and concubines, will be suddenly abandoned as one departs alone for the next world, with not a single person following. One lies cast upon the bed and pillow as a corpse, prostrate and supine; parents and wife and children beat their breasts and choke with sobs, while the multitude wails in longing, tearing out their hair and beating their heads. Though there is the sorrow of affectionate attachment during life, it ultimately leads to the pain of eternal separation."

Some are buried in tombs where flesh wastes away and bones rot; others have their corpses exposed as an offering of their bodies, with birds, beasts, and ants swarming over them to tear and pull at them. Some are cremated by fire, the stench and smoke billowing and choking the four directions, causing people to lament and grieve; they wail until their voices fail and return to their hometowns, leaving behind only ashes scattered by the wind and dust. Throughout their lives, their spirit soared alone above the clouds, yet in a single moment they take leave forever, trapped by frost and moonlight. They fight for the sake of wife and children, contending over wealth and profit until they are torn apart; they vie for prestige and lineage, binding themselves in resentment and retribution; they struggle for glory and splendor, harming the lives of others. Suddenly they pass away forever, falling eternally into the dark path, alone suffering the calamity of their own evil deeds while their wives and children remain safe and live in ease.
In the past, one committed evil solely for the sake of wife and children; yet when falling into the three miserable realms, who would have expected such solitary suffering?
How deeply lamentable! How deeply lamentable!
One must take heed! One must take heed!
This is called the suffering of death.
Regarding the sufferings of sorrow, lamentation, grief, and affliction, the *Śālistamba Sūtra* states:

"To feel regret for past events with a voice of mournful emotion is called sorrow (*śoka*); to have continuous recollection is called lamentation (*parideva*); to be oppressed by painful matters is called suffering (*duḥkha*); and to be bound by the entanglements of afflictions is called affliction (*upāyāsa*)."

The *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* states: "At the time of separation through death, the feverish mind of a fool who is greedily attached is called 'sorrow' (*śoka*); the raising of one's voice and weeping is called 'lamentation' (*parideva*); the contact of the five sense faculties [with their objects] is called 'pain' (*duḥkha*); the contact of the mental faculty [with its object] is called 'grief' (*daurmanasya*); and the intensification of grief and pain is called 'despair' (*upāyāsa*)."
Regarding those who undergo various sufferings for the sake of the five desires and material gain: birds lose their forms because of food, and humans lose their lives because of wealth.

The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states: "People of the world suffer when they have no fields or houses yet harbor desire; they also suffer when they possess fields and houses yet are stingy in guarding them. It is with all such five desires and material gains that it is thus: fearing the arbitrary encroachment of the five calamities and dreading the unjust seizure by neighbors, suffering arises."
The Sūtra says: "Furthermore, due to craving and attachment, one encounters the suffering of meeting with those one hates.
The Commentary states:
This refers to how stinginess and greed burn and oppress beings throughout the cycles of rebirth in the various realms of existence.

One becomes greedily attached to wealth already acquired and pursues that which has not yet been obtained; thus, manifold sufferings arise. The aforementioned five desires are likewise this suffering of not obtaining what one seeks.

In the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Śāstra*, the giving of the seven treasures filling worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges is explained as being inferior to upholding even a single four-line verse of this sutra. It states: "Afflictions arise from wealth as numerous as the motes of dust in the world; by upholding this sutra, these afflictions are extinguished. Therefore, the merit of giving wealth is small, while the merit of upholding the sutra is great."
The suffering of saṃsāra within the five destinies will be explained in the verses.

The hardship of poverty exists only among humans; however, the meeting with those one loves and the encounter with those one hates pertain to both humans and devas. This is exemplified by cases such as when a powerful son of heaven enters a celestial palace, seizes another's wife and children, and drives them out from that palace.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle four, fully explains the sufferings of the five destinies, including those of the devas.

The characteristics of the hells and other realms will be discussed in the verses [of this treatise]. Because the sensory objects within the human and heavenly realms are particularly exquisite, they involve much suffering from separation from the beloved (*priyaviprayoga-duḥkha*) and suffering from encountering the hated (*apriyasaṃprayoga-duḥkha*); therefore, these are specifically mentioned. One should extensively cite the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* to annotate this section, including matters such as the battles with the asuras.
Regarding the sūtra passage, “such various sufferings as these,” the commentary states: Thus far, the desire realm possesses all seven types of suffering.

The sufferings of the five destinies (*gati*) in the present and future lives possess the three types of suffering (*duḥkha*). In the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), there is only the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*) and the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*), because pleasure (*sukha*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*) exist there. The *Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra* cites a sūtra stating that “the form realm has the suffering of change” to mean that one enters a mind of transformation. In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there is only the single suffering of conditioned formations, because there is no feeling of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*) there.
The desire realm possesses all eight types of suffering, while the higher realms lack the first seven.
Regarding the Sūtra passage: "Sentient beings are submerged therein... yet they do not consider it a calamity," the commentary says:

Below, they are joined with and attached to worldly pleasures; they do not awaken through inferential knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), nor do they know through direct realization (*abhisamaya-jñāna*). They are neither startled by their effects nor terrified by their causes; they do not universally loathe suffering, nor do they seek liberation. Consequently, they rush and flow back and forth between the realms of good and evil without ever regarding it as a calamity. This is like a fool playing in filth, or like a child falling into a fiery furnace—neither feeling shame for the dust and grime, nor feeling pain from the burning fire.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from “Śāriputra” to “causing him to sport therein,” the commentary states:
This below corresponds to the demonstration that [the Great Vehicle] is not something to be sought after.
The preceding parables are fourfold:

first, the transformation of contemplating the fruit of the Mahāyāna; second, the transformation of recollecting the causes of the Mahāyāna; third, the transformation of manifesting the practices of the Mahāyāna accordingly; and fourth, the transformation of being without longing for or grasping at greatness.
This conjunction consists of three parts, which do not follow the order of the illustrations shown for the Mahāyāna practice and transformation:

first, the conjunction with the initial illustration; second, the passage beginning with "Śāriputra, the Tathāgata further acts... which conjoins with the second illustration; and third, the passage beginning with "Why is this so? which conjoins with the fourth illustration.
“Joy of the Buddha’s wisdom” refers to the power of the joined body, which suddenly uproots the various sufferings of the pratyekabuddhas as if with a table.

“Causing them to sport” refers to the power of the joined hands, which suddenly uproots the sufferings of the śrāvaka assembly as if with a garment’s fold. The intended meaning of this is: by means of the two sublime functions—the wisdom of the fruit of Buddhahood and great supernormal powers—one suddenly uproots the two vehicles and brings them forth from suffering.
Regarding the passage from "Śāriputra arrives" to "thereby attaining deliverance," the commentary states:
This is intended to inspire thoughts of the Mahāyāna through transformation.

Only through the single gate of the Bodhisattva can one emerge; yet if I were to suddenly bestow upon them wisdom and supernormal powers, and instead explain the Great Cause to transform these two sons, they would abandon the skillful means of teaching the Three Vehicles. Since the vessels of the Two Vehicles are small, they would be unable to practice accordingly and attain liberation from all suffering; as the gate would then be too narrow, they might well fall back into error.
This intention also warrants a secret discourse on matters of fear, so that they may not be burned or harmed by fire.
[The passage from] the Sūtra: "For what reason... up to the wisdom of a Buddha."
The commentary states:
This is the transformation of merging with the vastness that is free from desire for attainment.
Since the Buddha’s wisdom is already profound, by what means could it be fully understood?
Because the wisdom of the followers of the two vehicles is shallow, they do not aspire to or accept it.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from “Śāriputra... to the precious great chariot,” the commentary says:
The third major section, which concerns contemplating the means for deliverance, has two parts:
first, the analogy; second, the application.
This is the first part.

It is not by means of the power of his body of wisdom, nor by the power of his hands of supernormal faculties, but solely through the skillful means of verbal exhortation that he encourages and delivers his sons. Only after they have emerged from the house does he provide them with the great chariots. This demonstrates that one must cultivate sublime practices for oneself based on the Buddha as a condition to transcend birth and death; therefore, he extends this exhortation, for it is not by the Buddha's power alone that one can attain Buddhahood without cultivating the causes oneself.
"Exerting" (*mian*) means to encourage and stimulate.
Some editions read "exempting" (*mian*), which does not convey this meaning.
The sūtra says: "The Tathāgata likewise [establishes beings] in the Buddha-vehicle."
The commentary states:
This is a combined exposition.

It encompasses both wisdom (*jñāna*) and supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), yet it proceeds solely through skillful means (*upāya*) to exhort beings toward liberation from the three realms. The Buddha is like a skilled physician who prescribes medicine according to the illness; he merely uses skillful means to instruct them on how they should proceed. How could a skilled physician, while using his knife and hand to excise the disease within the abdomen, fail to provide medicine?
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "and spoke these words" to "then one will be burned," the commentary says:
The fourth major section below, which synthesizes the formal exposition of the Three Vehicles, has four parts:

First, there is the exhortation to weary of the three realms; second, the exhortation to take up the three vehicles; third, citing oneself as a witness; and fourth, praising the superior virtues of the vehicle.
This is the first [section].
"The burning house of the three realms" refers to its internal substance.
"The coarse and inferior five sensory objects" refer to external conditions.

One is exhorted to abandon both internal and external suffering; one must not give rise to craving and attachment toward the essence of the fruit, for through such craving and attachment, the afflictions burn and cook, causing further suffering and pain to arise. Thus, one is exhorted to renounce evil causes. Although there exists the wondrous fruit—the adamantine body internally and the pure land with its assembly of subtle five sensory objects externally—one should give rise to joyful aspiration toward them, yet this has not been explicitly stated.
The Sūtra says: "You should quickly exit the triple world and proceed to the Buddha-vehicle.
The commentary states:
This exhorts one to attain the three vehicles.
The Sūtra says: "I now [speak] for you... up to 'to entice and encourage sentient beings.
The commentary states:
This cites oneself as evidence.
"Preserving" (*bao*) means to be appropriate, to have faith, and to provide verification.
"Entrusting" (*ren*) means to preserve, to bring peace, to be acceptable, and to maintain.
To grant you this is to act as a guarantor, a source of faith, and a witness; it is to bring peace and allow for entrustment and maintenance, declaring that what is preserved shall never be in vain.

"Take them yourselves and do not give rise to doubt. The Dharma of the Three Vehicles is truly an excellent Dharma; I guarantee it for you. You should simply take it and apply yourself with diligent vigor. It is like when one buys goods in the world: if no one guarantees their authenticity, one knows the goods may not be genuine;
but if there is a guarantor, one should know they are superior goods. The Three Vehicles are likewise: I can guarantee them, but I cannot guarantee that birth and death are not real.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "He further spoke these words" to "there is nothing upon which to rely or seek," the commentary states:
This praises the superior virtues of the Vehicle.
The first part clarifies how this differs from birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), and the latter part clarifies the superior virtues of the vehicle.
This is the former.

The sages revile birth-and-death, while the sages of the Three Vehicles praise it; birth-and-death is characterized by bondage and the increase of afflictions (*kleśa*), resulting in a lack of mastery (*asvatantra*). Because the Three Vehicles are untainted (*anāsrava*), they are not bound and are thus termed "mastery" (*svatantra*).

Defiled phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) are termed "having a basis" (*sopadhi*). The fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*) depends on its cause for existence, and the cause of maturation depends on its fruit for its establishment. Among the defiled births and deaths, the superior realms are those of humans and devas; these possess objects of pursuit, which are known as the three kinds of seeking (*triṣaṃskāra*).
The three vehicles are not like this; they are not what is sought after. One seeks them because they are free from fault, not because they are faultless that one does not seek them.
The three types of seeking are:
first, the seeking of sensual desire (*kāma-īṣaṇā*); second, the seeking of existence (*bhava-īṣaṇā*); and third, the seeking of a false holy life (*mithyā-brahmacarya-īṣaṇā*).
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that those who fall into the pursuit of desire do so entirely for the sake of the three types of arising from desire, with neither addition nor subtraction.
These three arisings from desire are:
first, arising from the objects of desire while currently dwelling in them; this refers to humans and the gods from the Heaven of Contentment (*Tuṣita*) downward.
The second arises from objects of desire transformed by oneself; this is the fifth heaven of the desire realm.
The third arises from objects of desire transformed by others; this is the sixth heaven of the desire realm.
All those who fall into the pursuit of existence are born for the sake of these three kinds of pleasure.

First, his body is sprinkled with the joy and bliss born of seclusion; second, his body is sprinkled with the joy and bliss born of concentration; third, his body is sprinkled with the bliss born of the fading away of joy—these correspond respectively to the first, second, and third dhyānas.

Those who give rise to the desire for decline in the peaceful birthplaces of neither-suffering-nor-pleasure are extremely few; therefore, the fourth dhyāna is not established as a [distinct] birthplace.
Those who seek false brahmacarya refer to the various non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) who seek the four formless attainments (*ārūpya*) as the place of nirvāṇa and liberation.
Now, because these are not the three types of seeking, they are called "seeking nothing.

Although there is the seeking of the holy life (*brahmacarya*), because it is untainted (*anāsrava*), it is the unsurpassed, correct seeking for the holy life, and not the seeking for a false holy life.
The Sūtra says: "By means of these three vehicles, one reaches peace, security, and happiness. The commentary states: This section clarifies the supreme virtues of the vehicles.

Having correctly mounted the vehicle, one further delights oneself through the five faculties (*indriya*), the five powers (*bala*), the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), the eightfold path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*), the four dhyānas, the nine meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*), and the three samādhis. Thus, one attains immeasurable peace, security, and happiness; how could this possibly be like the manifold sufferings of saṃsāra?
Regarding the passage from "Śāriputra arrives" to "emerges from the burning house," the commentary states:
This constitutes the fourth major section below, which corresponds to the actual words regarding escaping the calamity.
The three vehicles are divided into three, each of which has two parts:
first the teaching (*dharma*), and later the synthesis.
This is the opening passage.
Each possesses four powers:
that which is the nature of internal wisdom is the power of the cause, because it is the seed-lineage by nature.

That which comes from the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is the power of the virtuous friend; for the Buddha serves as the condition. Encountering the Buddha—or failing to encounter him—one must initially rely upon the Buddha’s Dharma to be able to give rise to the resolve [for enlightenment], which is thus termed the power of the virtuous friend.
Hearing the Dharma and receiving it with faith is the power of mental attention (*manasikāra*), because it is the cultivation of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*).
Diligent and earnest exertion is the power of the provisions (*sambhāra*), for diligence is the foremost factor that encompasses all practices.
Relying on the four superior powers—causes, virtuous friends, mental attention, and provisions—one exclusively practices for oneself to seek nirvāṇa; this is called the Śrāvaka-yāna.

To hear the Dharma and practice it oneself without being able to transform others is called "seeking for oneself"; this does not mean one does not seek to become a Buddha, but rather acts as a disciple.

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* explains: "The sound of the holy teachings of all Buddhas is the foremost; because one hears these sounds of the teachings from teachers and friends and thereby realizes the fruit of holiness, one is called a Śrāvaka. This is a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound, meaning "one who hears the sound" (*śabda-śravaṇa*).

The *Śraddhādhimuktiparivarta* states: "Because they cause all to hear by means of the sound of the Buddha's teaching, they are called 'Hearers' (*śrāvaka*). This is explained either as a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent compound) or a *bahuvrīhi* (possessive compound).

The former refers to those with fixed lineage and the latter to those with unfixed lineage; for these seekers of nirvāṇa, the "all-encompassing wisdom" (*sarvajñajñāna*) that is studied is what constitutes the body of the chariot, not nirvāṇa itself.
Because this passage is abbreviated, the subsequent sections should be understood by analogy.
Regarding the sūtra passage: "If there are sentient beings... [until] they emerge from the burning house," the commentary says:
This involves only three powers, as the power of causes is omitted for brevity.
"Seeking spontaneous wisdom" means not seeking to appear in the world at the same time as a Buddha, because one does not attain the fruit only after having seen a Buddha.

As a sutra states: "When Śākyamuni appeared in the world, five hundred pratyekabuddhas emerged from the mountains and went to where the Buddha was. Thus, there is a community of pratyekabuddhas in the *Renyō-kyō* (Benevolent Kings Sutra) who, having already attained the Way prior to encountering the World-Honored One, do not attain the Way while in the presence of a Buddha like the śrāvakas; for this reason, they are said to be those who seek spontaneous wisdom (*svayambhū-jñāna*) through diligence and are able to realize the Path.

"One who delights in solitude and sublime tranquility" refers to the meaning of a Pratyekabuddha (Solitary Realizer); for, appearing in an age when no Buddha exists, they are able to realize the path and personally and perfectly realize the principle of nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, to use this wisdom to deeply understand the causes and conditions of all phenomena is the meaning of "Pratyekabuddha" (Solitary Realizer).

Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Alternatively, they are called Pratyekabuddhas because they realize the fruit of holiness by observing conditions, as they realize the fruit by contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination."
As for the *pratyekabuddha*, this is called the "Solitary Realizer. There are two types:
first, those who travel in groups; second, those who are like rhinoceros horns.
The former may see a Buddha, while the latter certainly do not.

Thus, the *Avataṃsaka* states: "When a Bodhisattva is in Tuṣita Heaven and is about to descend to be born, ten signs appear; the third is that he emits a great radiance from the palm of his right hand called 'Adorned and Purified World. If there are any Pratyekabuddhas within the trichiliocosm who encounter this light, they will swiftly enter nirvāṇa."
If they do not enter, by the power of the Buddha’s light, they will be transported to the buddha-fields of other directions and will not be able to see the Buddha.
It is clearly known that those who have completed a full hundred kalpas as pratyekabuddhas become rhinoceros-like [solitary realizers], and not those who travel in groups.

If one becomes a pratyekabuddha from the stage of the śrāvaka’s liberation-factor (mokṣabhāgīya), they become a rhinoceros-like (khaḍgaviṣāṇakalpa) pratyekabuddha; this may take up to a hundred kalpas because the time required is still long.
If one enters the four roots of goodness (catvāri nirvedhabhāgīyāni) as a pratyekabuddha, they become a group-dweller (vargacārin), because the remaining time is short.
Regarding "individually realized" (*pratyekabuddha*): [the term] is explained by the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) method as "one who awakens while depending on conditions.
In the Sūtra, from "If there are sentient beings... up to "...this is called the Mahāyāna," the commentary states:
In the initial exposition of the Dharma, there are two parts:
first, the explanation of the Mahāyāna, and second, the explanation of the Bodhisattvayāna.
This is the former.
"Omniscience" (sarvajñatā) refers to the wisdom that contemplates emptiness, which is common to all three vehicles.
"Buddha-wisdom" (buddhajñāna) refers to the wisdom that contemplates phenomena as having existence; this is uniquely accomplished by the Buddha alone.

Because these two types of wisdom arise from self-awakening, they are called "spontaneous wisdom" (*svayambhū-jñāna*); because they do not depend on external conditions, they are called "teacherless wisdom" (*aśaikṣa-jñāna*). Alternatively, the nature of wisdom is called spontaneous wisdom, while the characteristics of wisdom are called teacherless wisdom.

One seeks this knowledge, vision, retinue, powers, and fearlessnesses as internal virtues; externally, one is able to benefit sentient beings through compassion, bestowing happiness and providing aid by uprooting suffering—first with loving-kindness and subsequently with compassion.
The extensive and vast practice of understanding is called the Mahāyāna; the meaning of the term "Mahāyāna" has already been explained as above.
The Sūtra states: "Because the Bodhisattva seeks this vehicle, he emerges from the burning house."
The commentary states:
This explains the Bodhisattva vehicle and its analogies.
"Bodhisattva" is a general designation for those of the three vehicles.
If one seeks the designation "Mahāsattva" (Great Being) for this [bodhisattva], it is because they are a "great sentient being," whereas others do not receive this name.
As the *Prajñāpāramitopadeśa* by Asaṅga states:
"One is designated as a Mahāsattva due to being endowed with the seven kinds of greatness."

The "seeker of wisdom" (bodhi) is *buddha*, and the "one who possesses compassion" (*sattva*) is *sattva*; within these three vehicles, there are respectively those of one lineage and one caste, three lineages and two castes, and one lineage and three castes, due to the distinctions among the categories of definite and indefinite lineages.

The attainment of the fruit by those who first or last produce the thought of enlightenment is not fixed; for example, if Mahākāśyapa had not encountered the Buddha, he would have become a pratyekabuddha, but because he encountered the Buddha, he has now become a śrāvaka. The same principle may be inferred for Śāriputra and others.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra, "Śāriputra arrived and bestowed [the jewels] upon the sons," the commentary states:
The second major section below now explains the teaching of reality; it contains two parts:
First, the actual meaning is explained; second, doubts are resolved.
Of the four previous analogies, only two are now correlated here:
first, correlating [the analogy] to explain the fulfillment of the father’s intention, which begins with the words "These sentient beings... and so forth.
The subsequent passage, which states that the father gave only one,
does not accord with the text’s requirement for the sons to demand three, as this violates the sons' original intention.
This initial section further divides into two parts:
First the preceding parable is presented, and later it is applied to the Dharma.
Within the parable there are two parts:

first, seeing his son and being able to escape, his mind becomes tranquil; from "reflecting upon himself" (*svayam cintayati*) onwards, he fulfills the father’s intention—the meaning of which is clear.
Regarding the passage from the Sūtra, “The Tathāgata is also like this, up to ‘attaining the bliss of nirvāṇa,’” the commentary states:
The subsequent section on harmonizing with the father’s intention also has two parts.
First, by seeing their sons, they attain peace of mind; later, by explaining [the truth], they fulfill the father’s intent—this refers to the former.

Using the teaching as the gate, one emerges from the burning house and the perilous path of the triple world; using practice as the gate, one enters the fruit of nirvāṇa. Herein, there is only the gate of the teaching for emerging from the house, and the gate of practice is not mentioned. Yet the teaching can also lead to entry, because it enables one to enter the principle; thus, while this only speaks of emerging and not of entering, one may also say that attaining the bliss of nirvāṇa is itself what constitutes "entry."
The Sūtra states: "At that time, the Tathāgata went there and brought about his parinirvāṇa.
The commentary says:
This passage explains and fulfills the father’s intention.

Since there is no distinction between you, they should all equally receive the Mahāyāna; why should only Bodhisattvas be granted the Buddha’s extinction (nirvāṇa), while those of the two vehicles are not?
You should instead bring them to extinction through the Great Parinirvāṇa of the Buddha.
"Not causing" means there is no sense of causing [inequality]; it does not mean that one bodhisattva attains [the fruit] while other followers of the two vehicles do not.
This refers to the passage in the sutra from "all these sentient beings" up to "articles of entertainment."
The commentary states:
The following section corresponds to the "Father" chapter, but it contains only one [part], which is divided into two:
first, clarifying the body of the chariot; second, clarifying the virtues of the chariot.
This is the first point.

Regarding the phrase "endowed with all Buddhas," this refers to those of the two vehicles whose destiny is not yet fixed and those of the bodhisattva lineage; they are equally endowed with the meditative concentrations, liberations, and so forth of the Buddha-vehicle. Since the adornments of the One Vehicle are fully equipped with myriad virtues, these various instruments of enjoyment are mentioned here by way of abbreviation.
The Sūtra says: "All are of one characteristic, up to the supreme bliss.
The commentary states:
This clarifies the virtues of the vehicle; all these decorative ornaments and articles of enjoyment belong to this One Vehicle.

First, it is characterized by freedom from defilement; second, it belongs to the category of the untainted (*anāsrava*). Whether as cause or as fruit, it is praised by the noble ones, for it can produce for sentient beings the supreme, pure, and wondrous bliss of the untainted, being the source of all virtuous qualities.

Among the five types of happiness, there is no happiness free from affliction and harm; among the four types of happiness free from affliction, it is subsumed under the third, the joy of awakening to the Dharma, and the fourth, the joy of tranquility. It does not share the same merits as the sheep- and deer-carts of the two vehicles, for it is neither entirely free from defilement nor purely untainted (*anāsrava*). Although the noble ones may experience such happiness, they do not praise it as birth-happiness because it is not supreme; this is called the Mahāyāna.
In the Sūtra, it says: "Śāriputra, you shall not incur the fault of falsehood.
The commentary states:
The following section resolves doubts, which is twofold:
First the metaphor is presented, and later the doubts are resolved;
this is the first [section].
There are three parts to the preceding metaphor:
This refers to the question, the answer, and the seal.

Here, only the seal of approval is stated in its entirety, for it is adorned with jewels and endowed with all myriad virtues, and because it is the foremost in peace and security, being free from calamities and obstacles.
The Sūtra says: “The Tathāgata likewise goes there to deliver and liberate them.
The commentary states:
There are two [sections] below that correspond [to this].
First the thesis, then the explanation.
This is the thesis.
The Sūtra says: "For what reason... up to 'but they are not able to receive it all.'"
The commentary states:
This is the explanation.

My One Vehicle possesses immeasurable merit and can provide inexhaustible enjoyment for all sentient beings; yet, because sentient beings may possess either the nature for enlightenment or lack it, or possess a fixed nature or an unfixed nature, or may initially delight in the Lesser Vehicle and only later delight in the Great Vehicle, they are not all able to receive and uphold it in its entirety. Therefore, my initial teaching of the Three Vehicles and my present teaching of the One Reality are not false, as they are teachings designed to gradually lead them [to the truth].
Regarding the passage from “Śāriputra” up to “the detailed exposition of the three,” the commentary states:
This is the third major section, which provides the concluding response.

Based on the principles and conditions explained above, although the essence of the One Vehicle is differentiated and taught as three teachings, and the single ultimate fruit is spoken of as having three causes, in reality there are no three essences nor three ultimate fruits.

On the fourth day of the eleventh month of the same year, the punctuation was finalized using the manuscript from Ennyo-bō of Kōfuku-ji. Since the Kakushin manuscript is a punctuated edition, any discrepancies have been marked in vermilion; may this serve as a guide for future reference!
This is a manuscript written in black ink; it is the original text itself, as the red ink has not been applied.
